idiom_name: sealed interface/class + data class cases + exhaustive when
implementation_notes: Sealed classes and interfaces close the set at the module and package level (all direct subclasses must be declared there), and a when with a sealed subject is exhaustiveness-checked by the compiler, so the else branch is simply omitted and a new subclass becomes a compile error at every when that mentioned it (Kotlin spec, exhaustive when expressions). Data classes carry the variant payloads and object cases cover payload-free alternatives, so the accept()/visit() machinery of Visitor disappears; write when in expression position (val x = when (...)) to make the check mandatory. Keep polymorphic methods when the hierarchy is meant to be extended - sealed forbids subclasses outside the module - and remember that expect/actual multiplatform common code still needs an else, because platform subclasses are invisible there.
code_sketch:
sealed interface Shape
data class Circle(val r: Double) : Shape
data class Rect(val w: Double, val h: Double) : Shape
object Dot : Shape

fun area(s: Shape): Double = when (s) {       // exhaustive: no else needed
    is Circle -> Math.PI * s.r * s.r
    is Rect   -> s.w * s.h
    Dot       -> 1.0
}
pitfalls: sealed permits subclasses only in the module (and, historically, the package) that declares the sealed type, so a hierarchy another module must extend cannot be sealed.
A when used as a statement only warns when non-exhaustive; the check is mandatory in expression position, so binding the result is what makes the guarantee real.
In multiplatform expect/actual code the common module cannot see platform subclasses and the compiler requires an else - the coverage proof is lost exactly at that boundary.
